case_number: Criminal Appeal No 1260 of 2022 (Arising out of SLP (Crl) No 9836 of 2019)
summary: The case involved a dispute under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, where the respondent admitted signing a cheque but claimed it was a blank instrument given as security. The High Court allowed the respondent to engage a handwriting expert to examine whether the details in the cheque were filled by him. The Supreme Court held that Section 139 raises a rebuttable presumption that a cheque issued by a drawer is in discharge of a debt or liability. It ruled that the filling of cheque details by someone other than the drawer is immaterial; the liability persists unless the defence rebuts the presumption by preponderance of probabilities. Thus, the handwriting expert's opinion would not serve any purpose in rebutting the statutory presumption.
legal_provisions_cited: Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, (2019) 4 SCC 197
Anss Rajashekar v. Augustus Jeba Ananth, (2021) 5 SCC 283
final_judgment: Appeal allowed; impugned order permitting handwriting expert examination set aside; expert report not to be considered in trial; respondent's application for expert examination dismissed.
